stops.title: Walter Süskind Bridge
stops.subtitle: Drawbridge, built 1969-1972; renamed in 1972
stops.address: Nieuwe Herengracht / Amstel (linking Plantage to Weesperstraat), 1018 DG Amsterdam
stops.summary: A 5.5-metre-wide steel drawbridge spanning the Nieuwe Herengracht where it meets the Amstel. The bridge replaced an earlier iron drawbridge between 1969 and 1972 and was named in honour of Walter Süskind in 1972 — close to the route along which children from the crèche were carried out of the Plantage neighbourhood to safety. Today its bascule mechanism still opens for boat traffic; it is one of the better-known of Amsterdam's hundreds of working drawbridges.

facts.claim: Built 1969-1972; named for Walter Süskind.
facts.amplification: It crosses the Nieuwe Herengracht where it joins the Amstel river. The bridge is a working drawbridge; in 2017 its wooden deck was replaced with Accoya acetylated wood.

hero_image.credit: Wikimedia Commons — Amsterdam - boating on the canal (3411113235).jpg (CC license — see source)

gallery.credit: Rob Croes / Anefo (CC0 1.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: Unveiling of the Walter Süskind memorial plaque on bridge 237, 30 August 1972.
gallery.note: The unveiling of the memorial plaque on what was then bridge 237, on 30 August 1972 — the same year the wooden lift bridge over the Nieuwe Herengracht was renamed for him. Walter Süskind (1906–1945) was a German-Jewish refugee who became a key figure in saving roughly 600 children from the Hollandsche Schouwburg crèche.

gallery.credit: Rob Croes / Anefo (CC0 1.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: Wreath-laying at the unveiling of the Walter Süskind memorial plaque, August 1972.
gallery.note: Wreath-laying at the same 1972 unveiling. Süskind himself did not survive the war. After the crèche operation was discovered, he was deported with his wife Johanna and daughter Yvonne to Westerbork, then to Theresienstadt, and finally to Auschwitz; he died on a death march in early 1945, aged 39.

gallery.credit: Ceescamel (CC BY-SA 4.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: The Walter Süskind memorial plaque on bridge 237 today.
gallery.note: The plaque on the bridge today. The bridge connects the Nieuwe Keizersgracht to the Nieuwe Herengracht — directly across the Amstel from the former Jewish quarter. The location is symbolic: this is the route many of the smuggled children would have been taken along to safe houses outside the city.

gallery.credit: Michielverbeek (CC BY 4.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: The Walter Süskindbrug as a movable lift bridge across the Nieuwe Herengracht.
gallery.note: The Walter Süskindbrug today, a movable lift bridge in its raised position. The original 1972 wooden bridge was replaced by the current steel structure in 2021. The yellow Star of David carved into the railings — a deliberate choice in the rebuild — quotes the badge that the German occupier forced Dutch Jews to wear from May 1942.

gallery.credit: Dguendel (CC BY 4.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: The Walter Süskindbrug across the Nieuwe Herengracht.
gallery.note: The bridge in everyday use. Süskind's network at the crèche operated for nearly two years (October 1942 to September 1943) and saved an estimated 600 children — the largest single act of organised Jewish-and-Dutch rescue during the German occupation. He was posthumously honoured as Righteous Among the Nations in 2018.

gallery.credit: Fred Romero from Paris, France (CC BY 2.0) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: The Walter Süskind lift bridge, Amsterdam.
gallery.note: The Walter Süskindbrug. The bridge stands on the boundary between the old Jodenbuurt and the Plantage neighbourhood: most of the rescue work happened within a 200-metre radius of here, including the Hollandsche Schouwburg, the crèche, and the Hervormde Kweekschool teacher-training college.

gallery.credit: Alf van Beem (Public domain) via Wikimedia Commons
gallery.alt: The Walter Süskindbrug lit up at night.
gallery.note: The bridge at night. Süskind exploited his pre-war friendship with the German camp commander Ferdinand aus der Fünten and his fluency in German to negotiate a workable deception: he would 'forget' to register children, or quietly remove cards from the deportation list, while the Nazis believed he was a useful collaborator.

occupation_overview.title: Five years of occupation — context
occupation_overview.summary: Germany invaded the Netherlands on 10 May 1940. After five days of fighting and the destruction of central Rotterdam by aerial bombing on 14 May, the Dutch government surrendered. Initially everyday life changed little for most non-Jewish Dutch people, but a steady cascade of anti-Jewish measures began almost immediately and accelerated through 1941-42.

facts.claim: About 140,000 Jews lived in the Netherlands at the start of the war; about 79,000 in Amsterdam.
facts.amplification: Source doc gives '115,000 Jews in The Netherlands' and '85,000 lived in Amsterdam' — the standard figures from Anne Frank House, USHMM and the Dutch Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies (NIOD) are ~140,000 in NL and ~79,000 in Amsterdam in 1941. The 115,000 figure may exclude the ~25,000 German and Austrian refugees who arrived in the 1930s — but if so it should be ~110,000-115,000 'native' Dutch Jews; the Frank family is one of the refugee families and they are usually counted within the 140,000. Roughly 75% — 102,000 — were murdered, the highest proportion of any country in Western Europe.
